data.hypothesis: The earlier 4096-elements-per-CTA, 768-CTA-cap candidate measured 8.017 µs, while 8192/512 measured 6.341 µs; these do not isolate whether work per CTA or CTA count drove the difference. This experiment holds the 4096 target fixed and raises the cap to 1024, giving 1024 CTAs at n=2^22. More CTAs may improve input throughput enough to offset additional output-atomic contention.

memory_lessons.applicability: The measured configurations differ in more than one parameter, so they motivate a controlled test but do not establish a monotonic CTA-count or work-per-CTA effect.
memory_lessons.claim: The 4096/768 candidate averaged 8.017 µs and the 8192/512 candidate averaged 6.341 µs; the performance gap cannot be attributed to either CTA count or per-CTA work alone.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Keep the 4096-elements-per-CTA target and test a 1024-CTA cap; compare repeated timings and checks with these candidates and the baseline.

data.notes: The visible catalog has four distinct valid candidate programs and no repeats; its 4096/768 result did not beat 8192/512. The baseline hierarchical program is valid at 46.672 µs over three samples. The proposed large-input branch zeroes output and reduces on the same default stream, without initialized scratch; smaller positive sizes retain the hierarchical path and nonpositive sizes are zeroed. These are controller facts and a testable hypothesis, not a speed claim. No commands were executed.
transformations: Add a one-thread output-zeroing kernel and a 256-thread, grid-stride reduction kernel that accumulates with unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, reduces within each CTA, and performs one int32 atomicAdd per CTA.
For n >= 2^20, launch the zeroing kernel and then the reduction in the same default stream; choose ceil(n/4096) CTAs capped at 1024.
Retain the hierarchical reduction for positive sizes below the threshold and explicitly zero the output for n <= 0.
